title: Structure: Sequence of Tenses and Reported Speech
summary: How tenses, pronouns and time words change when speech is reported, the back-shift rule, the exceptions and worked examples.

p: When we report what someone said, we often change the tense. If the reporting verb (said, told, explained, asked) is in the past, the verb in the reported clause usually moves one step back into the past.

head: Direct speech
Reported speech
rows: Simple past: He said he worked here.
Past continuous: He said he was working.
Past perfect: He said he had finished.
Past perfect: He said he had finished it.

sections.h: Changes in time and place words
p: now becomes then; today becomes that day; tomorrow becomes the next day or the following day; yesterday becomes the day before or the previous day; this becomes that; these becomes those; here becomes there. Pronouns also change to fit the reporter's view.

If the reporting verb is in the present (says, explains), or if the reported fact is still true or is a general truth, the tense need not change. Direct: 'I am 16 years old.' Reported: 'He says he is 16.' or 'He said he is 16.' 'She said the Earth revolves around the sun.'

Direct: 'I cannot attend the meeting tomorrow because I have a doctor's appointment,' she said. Reported: She said that she could not attend the meeting the following day because she had a doctor's appointment.

activity: Report: 'I will call you later,' he said. (He said that he would call me later.) 'I am reading a fascinating book,' John said. 'We visited our grandparents last weekend,' they told me. 'The train will arrive at 8 PM,' the announcement stated. 'You must complete this form today,' the secretary said to me. (John said he was reading a fascinating book; they told me they had visited their grandparents the previous weekend; the announcement stated that the train would arrive at 8 PM; the secretary told me that I had to complete that form that day.)

title: Comprehension: Reading for Critical Evaluation
summary: The critical reader's questions: purpose, tone, bias, strength of argument (including two logical fallacies) and reliability of the source.

p: Critical evaluation goes beyond understanding to analysing and judging a text: examining the argument, spotting bias and weighing the evidence. It makes you a discerning reader.
1. Author's purpose: to inform (news, textbook), to persuade (opinion piece, advertisement, speech), to entertain (novel, comic strip) or to satirise (use humour to criticise).
2. Author's tone: objective and neutral (facts, little emotion), subjective and emotional (loaded language, exclamation marks), or sarcastic, angry, enthusiastic or dismissive.

3. Author's bias: a pre-formed opinion that affects fairness. Look for loaded language ('heroic freedom fighters' against 'ruthless terrorists'), one-sided argument, missing key facts or heavy emotional appeals.

4. Validity of the argument: is it based on facts, statistics and examples, or on personal stories and feelings? Watch for logical fallacies, such as ad hominem (attacking the person instead of the argument) and hasty generalisation (a big claim from a small sample).
5. Reliability of the source: is the author an expert? Is the publication reputable, or a personal blog? Is it checked by experts (peer-reviewed)?

activity: Find a short opinion article or letter to the editor. Write 150 to 200 words that say (a) the author's main purpose; (b) the tone, with one quoted phrase as proof; (c) one possible bias or one piece of evidence used.

title: Writing: Articles for a Public Audience
summary: How to write a magazine or newspaper article with a headline, by-line, hooking opening, structured body and conclusion, and how it differs from a formal letter.

p: An article is a piece written for a newspaper, magazine or online platform. Unlike a formal letter, it speaks to a wide public audience. Its purpose may be to inform, persuade or entertain, and its tone can be set to match.

1. Headline: catchy and engaging, giving a clear idea of the content (for example 'The Silent Epidemic: Fighting Loneliness in a Hyper-Connected World'). 2. By-line: the author's name, sometimes with a role (By Adeola Samuel, SS2 student and youth columnist). 3. Introduction (the hook): grab attention at once with a surprising statistic, a rhetorical question, a short story or a bold statement. 4. Body: several paragraphs, each on one main idea, with facts, examples, quotations and reasoning. 5. Conclusion: a satisfying ending: sum up, offer a solution, make a prediction or end with a call to action.
Study the table.

title: Structure: Active and Passive Voice
summary: The difference between active and passive voice, the rules for changing one to the other and a table of conversion for each tense.

p: Voice shows how the verb's action relates to the subject and object. Active voice: the subject performs the action ('The dog chased the cat'). Passive voice: the subject receives the action ('The cat was chased by the dog'); the focus is on the action or receiver, not the doer. The passive is common in formal and scientific writing.

1. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive. 2. The verb becomes a form of 'to be' + the past participle (am, is, are, was, were, be, being, been). 3. The old subject becomes the agent introduced by 'by', or is left out if unknown or unimportant ('Someone has stolen my bicycle' becomes 'My bicycle has been stolen').
Study the table.

head: Tense
Active
Passive
rows: The letter is written by him.
The letter is being written by him.
The letter has been written by him.
The letter was written by him.
The letter was being written by him.
The letter had been written by him.
The letter will be written by him.
The letter can be written by him.

p: Active: 'The chef is preparing the meal.' The object 'the meal' becomes the subject; 'is preparing' (present continuous) becomes 'is being prepared'; the subject becomes the agent 'by the chef'. Passive: 'The meal is being prepared by the chef.'

activity: Change to passive: 'The company will launch the new product next month' (The new product will be launched by the company next month); 'The students are reading the books' (The books are being read by the students); 'Someone has stolen my bicycle' (My bicycle has been stolen); 'The government must address this issue' (This issue must be addressed by the government). Change to active: 'The window was broken by the children' (The children broke the window); 'A new shopping centre is being built in our town' (They are building a new shopping centre in our town).

title: Oral English: Recognising Stress Patterns
summary: Primary and secondary stress, common patterns in two- and three-syllable words and the effect of suffixes on stress.

p: A stressed syllable is louder, longer and often higher. Primary stress is the strongest, marked with a high vertical line (ˈ) before the syllable. Secondary stress is weaker, marked with a low vertical line (ˌ). Wrong stress can make a word hard to understand.
Two-syllable words: stress on the first syllable (often nouns and adjectives): TAble, MOTHer, HAPpy; stress on the second (often verbs): preSENT, reCORD, deCIDE.
Three-syllable words: first syllable: HOSpital, MANagement; second: toMORrow, conDItion; third: engiNEER, volunTEER.

Suffixes that shift stress: -tion, -sion, -ic, -ity: the stress falls on the syllable before the suffix: inforMAtion, deCIsion, ecoNOmic, aBILity. Suffixes that usually do not change the stress of the root: -ful, -less, -ness, -ly (BEAUtiful, HOPEless).

Your lesson notes say that 'MUSic' becomes 'muSIcal'. That is not right: the stress stays on the first syllable in 'MUsical'. Words like 'MEMory' and 'MEMorise' also keep the first-syllable stress. When in doubt, check the stress in a dictionary.

title: Revision
summary: A summary of the term's grammar, oral English, writing, comprehension and vocabulary with practice tasks.

p: Possessive apostrophe: singular 's; plural in s '; irregular plural 's; joint (John and Mary's house) and separate (John's and Mary's houses); 'its' (possessive) against 'it's' (it is). Punctuation: colon after a complete clause to introduce; semi-colon to join related clauses or separate complex list items; hyphen in compound modifiers before a noun. Sentence types: declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory. Pronouns: subject and object case, 'between you and me'; who, whom, whose, which, that. Reported speech: back-shift and changes of time words. Phrasal verbs: put up with, look up to, get away with, come up with, run out of. Active and passive voice across tenses.

Voiced and voiceless pairs (pat, bat; safe, save; price, prize). Intonation: falling for statements, commands and wh-questions; rising for yes/no questions, politeness, uncertainty and non-final list items; high-rising for surprise; fall-rise for doubt. Rhyme scheme: AABB, ABAB, ABBA, ABCB. Stress: two-syllable nouns first, verbs second; before -tion, -ic, -ity.

Formal letter of complaint: address, date, recipient, salutation, heading, purpose-problem-remedy, 'Yours faithfully', signature, name. Informal letter: address, date, first-name salutation, flexible body, friendly closing. Short story: plot, character, setting, conflict, theme. Article: headline, by-line, hook, body, conclusion; no addresses or salutation.

Main point and topic sentence; implied meaning (inference); note-making with abbreviations and an outline; critical evaluation: purpose, tone, bias, validity, reliability. Vocabulary: words of the week and the registers of the press, the environment, building and technology.

Correct: 'The childrens toys were scattered' (children's). Punctuate: 'She needed the following items a passport a ticket and a suitcase' (items: a passport, a ticket and a suitcase). Choose: 'The person (who / whom) I met was friendly' (whom). Report: 'I will finish the project tomorrow,' she said (She said she would finish the project the next day). Passive: 'The company is launching a new product' (A new product is being launched by the company). Mark the stress: information, ability, understand, political.
